title: Polyuria and Hyponatremia: Water Deprivation, Copeptin and SIAD
summary: Learn how the water deprivation test and copeptin separate central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and primary polydipsia, and why low sodium with concentrated urine is not SIAD until volume, urine sodium and other causes are checked.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 25 Hit 7 (water deprivation/desmopressin test; urine sodium in hyponatremia), Hit 8 (copeptin cut-offs) and Trap 5 (hyponatremia with concentrated urine), checked against Refardt 2019, Flynn 2024, Warren 2023 and Arima 2022. Hit 7’s “central = >10% rise, nephrogenic = <10%” is replaced by the classic Miller criteria (>50% rise for complete central; >9% separates partial central from primary polydipsia; register flag rv-desmopressin-rise-cutoffs). Hit 8’s ≤4.9/>4.9 cut-off is taught as valid only after osmotic (hypertonic saline) stimulation (register flag rv-copeptin-stimulated-only). Trap 5’s “fractional sodium excretion >0.5% favours renal salt wasting” is not taught: the source read describes fractional uric acid excretion instead and notes cerebral salt wasting has no standardized criteria (register flag rv-siad-fena-salt-wasting). Not taught: treatment, arginine-stimulated copeptin, nephrogenic SIAD.

objectives: Explain why copeptin is used as a stable surrogate for vasopressin.
Interpret water deprivation/desmopressin results and resting and hypertonic-saline-stimulated copeptin in polyuria.
Apply the diagnostic criteria for SIAD and name the causes that must be excluded.

scenes.title: Too much water, too little sodium
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients. (1) A 30-year-old passing about 6 L of dilute urine a day, plasma sodium 142 mmol/L, baseline copeptin 3 pmol/L. (2) A patient taking lithium with the same polyuria, baseline copeptin 35 pmol/L without thirsting. (3) An inpatient taking a thiazide diuretic: sodium 126 mmol/L, urine osmolality 450 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 45 mmol/L, looks euvolemic. Question token: “Central, nephrogenic, polydipsia, or SIAD?”

cues.text: Three invented patients. The first passes six litres of dilute urine a day; normal sodium; copeptin three picomoles per litre.
The second takes lithium, has the same polyuria, and a resting copeptin of thirty-five.
The third has a sodium of one hundred twenty-six, concentrated urine, a high urine sodium, and takes a thiazide. Which is central, nephrogenic, polydipsia, or inappropriate antidiuresis?

scenes.title: ADH, its receipt, and three causes of polyuria
scenes.altText: Schematic loop: rising plasma osmolality (and, as a non-osmotic stimulus, falling blood volume) triggers arginine vasopressin (AVP, ADH) release from the posterior pituitary; AVP acts on kidney V2 receptors so aquaporin-2 channels reabsorb water. Copeptin card: the C-terminal piece of the same precursor, released in equal amounts to AVP; AVP itself is hard to measure, while copeptin is a stable sandwich-immunoassay analyte (<20% loss after 7 days at room temperature). Polyuria-polydipsia card: >50 mL/kg/24 h of urine; after excluding osmotic diuresis the causes are central DI (too little AVP), nephrogenic DI (kidney resistance; genetic, electrolyte disorders, drugs such as lithium) and primary polydipsia (too much drinking). Name card: a 2022 working group proposed AVP deficiency (AVP-D) and AVP resistance (AVP-R).

cues.text: When plasma osmolality rises, the posterior pituitary releases vasopressin, also called ADH. It acts on V2 receptors in the kidney, and aquaporin-2 channels pull water back.
Vasopressin is hard to measure reliably. Copeptin is cut from the same precursor in equal amounts, and it is stable in the tube, so it works as a receipt for vasopressin release.

Polyuria means more than fifty millilitres per kilogram of urine a day. Once osmotic diuresis is excluded, there are three causes: too little vasopressin, which is central diabetes insipidus; kidneys that ignore it, which is nephrogenic, for example from lithium; and simply drinking too much, primary polydipsia.
Newer names: a 2022 working group proposed vasopressin deficiency and vasopressin resistance for the central and nephrogenic forms.

scenes.title: Water deprivation versus copeptin
scenes.altText: Water deprivation card: fluids stopped; test ends at 17 hours, plasma sodium ≥150 mmol/L, or 3–5% weight loss; then desmopressin (synthetic AVP) is given. Classic Miller interpretation: urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg on thirsting plus a >50% rise after desmopressin = complete central DI; a smaller rise = nephrogenic DI; 300–800 mOsm/kg = partial central DI or primary polydipsia, with a >9% rise favouring partial central. Accuracy card: these cut-offs came from a small cohort and reached only 77% accuracy in a 156-patient study. Copeptin card: baseline copeptin >21.4 pmol/L without thirsting = nephrogenic DI; otherwise stimulate with 3% hypertonic saline to sodium ≥150 mmol/L (>147 suggested in practice): stimulated copeptin >4.9 pmol/L = primary polydipsia, ≤4.9 = central DI (97% correct).

cues.text: The classic test is water deprivation. Fluids stop until seventeen hours pass, sodium reaches one hundred fifty, or three to five percent of body weight is lost. Then desmopressin, synthetic vasopressin, is given.

Classic reading: urine stays below three hundred, then rises more than fifty percent after desmopressin, complete central. A smaller rise points to nephrogenic. Between three hundred and eight hundred, a rise above nine percent favours partial central over primary polydipsia. These cut-offs were only seventy-seven percent accurate in a large study.
Copeptin simplifies this. A resting copeptin above twenty-one point four picomoles per litre, without thirsting, identifies nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Otherwise, raise the sodium with hypertonic saline. A stimulated copeptin above four point nine means primary polydipsia; at or below four point nine means central. That was correct in ninety-seven percent of patients.

scenes.title: Hyponatremia with concentrated urine
scenes.altText: SIAD criteria card (Bartter–Schwartz, as tabulated in Warren 2023): plasma osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg; clinical euvolemia; urine sodium >30 mmol/L with normal salt and water intake; no glucocorticoid insufficiency or severe hypothyroidism; normal renal function and no diuretic use. Mimic card: urine sodium <30 mmol/L points to low effective volume (saline-responsive); diuretics and adrenal insufficiency also give a high urine sodium; copeptin is of little diagnostic value in SIAD. Hook answers: (1) baseline copeptin low → needs hypertonic saline stimulation; (2) resting copeptin 35 (>21.4) on lithium → nephrogenic DI; (3) on a thiazide → cannot call SIAD until the diuretic is accounted for.

cues.text: Now the opposite problem: low sodium with concentrated urine. Inappropriate antidiuresis needs low plasma osmolality, urine osmolality above one hundred, a euvolemic patient, and urine sodium above thirty on a normal salt intake.

It is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out cortisol deficiency, severe hypothyroidism, kidney failure and diuretics. A urine sodium below thirty points to low volume instead. And copeptin adds little here.

Back to the hook. Patient one has a low resting copeptin, so the next step is hypertonic saline stimulation. Patient two, on lithium, with a resting copeptin of thirty-five, fits nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Patient three takes a thiazide, which also raises urine sodium, so inappropriate antidiuresis cannot be called yet.

props.title: SIAD needs all of these
lines: No adrenal, thyroid, renal, diuretic cause

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Any >10% rise after desmopressin = central DI” (✓ classic criteria: >50% rise for complete central; the ~9% cut separates partial central from primary polydipsia); “Random copeptin ≤4.9 = central DI” (✓ the 4.9 cut-off applies only after osmotic stimulation; at rest, only >21.4 is diagnostic, for nephrogenic DI); “Low sodium + concentrated urine = SIADH” (✓ needs euvolemia, urine sodium >30 and exclusion of adrenal, thyroid, renal and diuretic causes).

cues.text: Trap one: any rise above ten percent after desmopressin means central. No: complete central needs a rise above fifty percent; the small cut-off only separates partial central from primary polydipsia.
Trap two: a random copeptin at or below four point nine means central. No: that cut-off works only after hypertonic saline.
Trap three: low sodium with concentrated urine means inappropriate antidiuresis. No: check volume, urine sodium, and adrenal, thyroid, kidney and diuretic causes first.

scenes.title: Copeptin is the receipt
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Vasopressin is cash spent fast; copeptin is the receipt printed with every sale. A big receipt pile at rest means the kidney shop keeps paying and gets nothing (nephrogenic). Push the till with hypertonic saline: no receipts means the cashier never sold (central); receipts mean the till works and the customer just drinks a lot (primary polydipsia).” Tokens: high at rest = nephrogenic · low after saline = central · normal after saline = polydipsia. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: vasopressin is cash spent fast; copeptin is the receipt printed with every sale. A pile of receipts at rest: the kidney is not listening, nephrogenic. After a hypertonic saline push, no receipts means central, and receipts mean primary polydipsia.
Where it breaks: the low cut-off only works after osmotic stimulation; illness and stress raise copeptin on their own; and copeptin is of little use in inappropriate antidiuresis.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Resting copeptin > 21.4 = nephrogenic · after 3% saline: ≤ 4.9 central, > 4.9 polydipsia”, “SIAD = euvolemic, Uosm > 100, UNa > 30, exclusions done”.

cues.text: Use a high resting copeptin to spot nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, use copeptin after hypertonic saline to separate central diabetes insipidus from primary polydipsia, and call low sodium with concentrated urine inappropriate antidiuresis only in a euvolemic patient with high urine sodium after adrenal, thyroid, kidney and diuretic causes are excluded.

props.label: SIAD = euvolemic · Uosm > 100 · UNa > 30 · exclusions done

explanation.what: Plain language: vasopressin (ADH) tells the kidney to keep water. Too little of it, or a kidney that ignores it, makes large volumes of dilute urine; drinking too much does the same. Too much of it at the wrong time dilutes the blood sodium. Copeptin is a stable fragment made alongside vasopressin, so labs measure it instead. Scientific terms: arginine vasopressin (AVP), V2 receptor, aquaporin-2, copeptin, polyuria-polydipsia syndrome, central diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency), nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (AVP resistance), primary polydipsia, water deprivation test, desmopressin, hypertonic saline stimulation, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD).
explanation.why: AVP is hard to measure reliably, so the classic test inferred it indirectly from urine osmolality, with limited accuracy. Copeptin is released in equal amounts to AVP and is stable ex vivo, so it can be measured directly, at rest or after osmotic stimulation. In hyponatremia, many conditions concentrate the urine, so SIAD can only be diagnosed after volume status, urine sodium and other causes are assessed.
explanation.measure: Polyuria: >50 mL/kg/24 h. Water deprivation: stop at 17 h, sodium ≥150 mmol/L or 3–5% weight loss, then desmopressin; urine osmolality <300 with >50% rise = complete central; smaller rise = nephrogenic; 300–800 with >9% rise favours partial central over primary polydipsia (77% accuracy in a 156-patient study). Copeptin: resting >21.4 pmol/L without thirsting = nephrogenic; after 3% saline to sodium ≥150 (≥147 suggested in practice), >4.9 pmol/L = primary polydipsia, ≤4.9 = central (97% correct). SIAD: plasma osmolality <275, urine osmolality >100, euvolemia, urine sodium >30 on normal intake, no glucocorticoid insufficiency or severe hypothyroidism, normal renal function, no diuretics.
explanation.differs: Central (little AVP; responds to desmopressin) vs nephrogenic (high copeptin at rest; little response) vs primary polydipsia (normal stimulated copeptin). SIAD (euvolemic, urine sodium >30) vs hypovolemic hyponatremia (urine sodium usually <30) vs diuretic or adrenal-insufficiency hyponatremia (high urine sodium, but excluded by the criteria).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpret a resting or stimulated copeptin, read a desmopressin response, or recognise that concentrated urine with hyponatremia does not equal SIAD when the patient is hypovolemic, on a diuretic, or cortisol-deficient.

mnemonic.text: Vasopressin is cash spent fast; copeptin is the receipt printed with every sale. Lots of receipts at rest: the kidney shop is paid but not listening (nephrogenic). After a hypertonic saline push: no receipts = central; receipts = primary polydipsia.
mnemonic.explanation: Links copeptin to AVP release and orders the two copeptin decisions.
mnemonic.limitation: The 4.9 pmol/L cut-off applies only after osmotic stimulation; stress and acute illness raise copeptin non-specifically; copeptin is of little diagnostic value in SIAD.

analogyLimitations: Cut-offs come from specific studies and assays; local protocols may differ.
takeaway: Use a high resting copeptin to spot nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, use copeptin after hypertonic saline to separate central diabetes insipidus from primary polydipsia, and call low sodium with concentrated urine inappropriate antidiuresis only in a euvolemic patient with high urine sodium after adrenal, thyroid, kidney and diuretic causes are excluded.

questions.stem: A patient taking lithium has polyuria of about 5 L/day. A resting plasma copeptin, drawn without prior thirsting, is 35 pmol/L. Which diagnosis does this support?

options.rationale: Correct. A resting copeptin above 21.4 pmol/L identifies nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; lithium is a recognised drug cause.
Incorrect. Central diabetes insipidus has low copeptin, especially after osmotic stimulation.
Incorrect. Primary polydipsia is identified by a stimulated copeptin above 4.9 pmol/L, not by a very high resting value.

options.text: Nothing yet; the 4.9 pmol/L cut-off must be applied after hypertonic saline
options.rationale: Incorrect. Stimulation is needed only when the resting copeptin is not above 21.4 pmol/L.

questions.stem: At the end of a water deprivation test, urine osmolality is 180 mOsm/kg. One hour after desmopressin it is 420 mOsm/kg. Using the classic criteria, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. Urine osmolality stayed below 300 on thirsting and rose by more than 50% (about 133%) after desmopressin.
Incorrect. The kidney responded strongly to desmopressin, so it is not resistant to AVP.
Incorrect. Primary polydipsia typically concentrates to 300–800 mOsm/kg on thirsting, with little further rise.
Incorrect. Healthy people concentrate urine above 800 mOsm/kg when deprived of water.

questions.stem: A clinically euvolemic patient has serum sodium 125 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 262 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 410 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 50 mmol/L, and takes hydrochlorothiazide. Which statement is correct?

options.text: SIAD cannot be diagnosed yet, because diuretic use must be excluded and thiazides also raise urine sodium
options.rationale: Correct. The SIAD criteria require absence of diuretic use; thiazides can mimic SIAD.

options.text: SIAD is confirmed, because urine osmolality is above 100 and urine sodium above 30
options.rationale: Incorrect. These criteria are necessary but not sufficient; diuretics, glucocorticoid insufficiency, severe hypothyroidism and renal failure must be excluded.
Incorrect. Copeptin levels overlap widely across causes of hyponatremia and are of little diagnostic value in SIAD.

options.text: The high urine sodium proves hypovolemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hypovolemia usually gives a urine sodium below 30 mmol/L.

claims.text: AVP physiology; copeptin equimolar and stable as an AVP surrogate; polyuria definition and three causes.
Proposed names AVP deficiency and AVP resistance.
Water deprivation endpoints and classic desmopressin-response criteria; 77% accuracy.
Resting copeptin >21.4 pmol/L = nephrogenic DI; stimulated copeptin 4.9 pmol/L separates central DI from primary polydipsia after hypertonic saline.
SIAD criteria, exclusions, urine sodium threshold, mimics; copeptin of little value in SIAD.
Reviewer: fractional sodium excretion >0.5% favours renal salt wasting over SIAD.
claims.note: Not taught. The source read discusses fractional uric acid excretion and states cerebral salt wasting has no standardized diagnostic criteria.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 25 Hit 7 gives central DI as a >10% and nephrogenic DI as a <10% rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin. The classic (Miller) criteria summarised by Refardt 2019 and Flynn 2024 use a >50% rise for complete central DI; a ~9% cut separates partial central DI from primary polydipsia; these cut-offs were small-cohort derived and only 77% accurate (register flag rv-desmopressin-rise-cutoffs).

Ch. 25 Hit 8 lists copeptin ≤4.9 pmol/L = central DI and >4.9 = primary polydipsia without stating that this cut-off applies only after osmotic stimulation (hypertonic saline to sodium ≥150 mmol/L); resting values of central DI and primary polydipsia overlap (Refardt 2019; register flag rv-copeptin-stimulated-only).

Ch. 25 Trap 5 says fractional sodium excretion >0.5% favours renal salt wasting. Warren 2023 instead discusses fractional uric acid excretion and states cerebral salt wasting has no standardized criteria; the FENa rule is not taught (register flag rv-siad-fena-salt-wasting).
The chapter uses “central/nephrogenic diabetes insipidus”; a 2022 international working group proposed AVP deficiency and AVP resistance (Arima 2022). The lesson teaches both names.
